b.x: Staying home is still plan A most of the time. This kit is for when the building, the flood, or the blackout sends you across the city. It is not a weapon, not a uniform, not a photo. 192, 193 and 190 are valid in Brazil. Outside the country, they are different. The 72-hour bag, in detail, stays beside this. Here what changes is what the street demands.

In the woods the error is thirst and cold. In the city the error is stairs, a crowd, a card that will not pass, and a patrol look. The elevator stops. The turnstile will not take the campaign pack. The pharmacy closes. The bus stop floods. The danger lives in the corridor, the gap, the polite request, not in the animal. The urban kit fits what you already cross every day: work, the market, someone’s house. If it draws eyes at the bakery, it failed before it served.

A work bag, a class bag, or a short-trip bag. The color of the street. No molle, no patch, no skull. What goes on the body: the shoe you have already walked in, not the new boot. A thin poncho in the outer pocket, because the rain starts in the middle of the block. Photo ID in the front pocket, not at the bottom. Keys. Small cash in small notes: bakery change, not a wad. One card, knowing the machine may be mute. A small light. A charged phone, a short cable, a power bank. The next 24 hours of medicine in the pocket, the rest in the bag.

Two to three liters if you walk. One liter, one kilo. In the city you do not drink from the avenue creek. The refill plan is people and a known tap: home, work, the meeting-point house. A filter or tablets go in if the way passes doubtful water or a flood. A boil is not done in the building corridor. A smell of gas, the flame waits. The car water, if the car is plan B, changes in the heat. A bottle that closes, inside a bag, so it does not wet the document when the pack tips on the bus.

What you eat standing up, with no stove, no smell, no plate. A bar, nuts, a biscuit the house already eats, one can only if the opener is in the bag and you have a place to sit without an audience. Three days at most. It is not the apartment store: that stays in the pantry, with rotation. On the street, too much food is weight and it is talk. Sugar only for someone awake who swallows. If there is a child, the snack they accept on Tuesday, not the new bar from the ad.

A copy of the ID, the health card, the prescription. The original stays in the pocket if you have to show it. Contacts on paper: meeting point, deadline, one phone outside the neighborhood. Two walking routes that are not the same street. The hospital and the pharmacy that still know your name, marked on the paper map, not only in the app. An offline map tested in airplane mode, of the whole region, not of one block. The emergency numbers written. In Brazil, 192, 193, 190. Outside, the local number, before you need it. A notebook and a pencil. Ink dies in the rain.
Body in the rain and on the stairs

A poncho. A dry sock in a bag. One discreet change of clothes, not a uniform. A thin blanket if the night may be in the car or in a shelter. Soap, paper, a pad, a trash bag. Gloves and gauze, the aid that fits, not the house box. The daily medicine for 72 hours, with the dose. Simple work gloves if the way has flood debris, with no operation look. A whistle. A torch that is not the phone. A small battery radio, because the city tower falls too. The elevator is not a plan. Three flights with the bag on your back, or something comes out.

Camouflage, a vest, combat boots, a patch, a shop-window knife, a hatchet, too much rope, a stove to use on the stairs. That describes you to whoever is looking. A fire steel does not cook the corridor rice. A weapon is not a kit item in this guide and it is not an identity. Do not film the route. Do not post the bag. Do not discuss the plan in the elevator. The tool, if one exists, is legal, small, and disappears in the pocket. Movement on the street, what to do when someone asks you to stop, is in the urban-movement field. The kit does not replace that eye.

The bag stays at the door, not at the back of the bedroom. Once a month, put it on and walk fifteen minutes on one of the two routes, by day, without telling anyone on the street. See where the water rises, where the sidewalk breaks, where there are people and light. If the shoulder hurts, weight came out. If you cannot find the document without stopping, the bag is wrong. In the heat, change the water. With the season, change the child’s clothes. Whoever lives with you knows the sentence of the point and does not argue it in the hour the stairs get wet. No audience.
